semantic_correction.stem: After abdominal surgery, a client coughs and the incision opens with bowel visible through the wound. Which action should the nurse take?

options.A: Cover the exposed bowel with sterile gauze moistened with saline and obtain urgent surgical evaluation.
options.B: Using sterile gloves, gently return the exposed bowel to the abdominal cavity and apply a pressure dressing.
options.C: Cover the incision with dry sterile gauze, apply an abdominal binder, and reassess after the client rests.
options.D: Irrigate the exposed bowel with antiseptic solution, pack the incision with gauze, and reinforce the dressing.

semantic_correction.rationale: Current NCBI/StatPearls guidance identifies bowel evisceration through an abdominal fascial defect as a true surgical emergency. When evisceration occurs, the exposed bowel should be covered or wrapped with gauze moistened with saline to prevent fluid loss and the client should receive emergent surgical evaluation and operative management. The nurse should not attempt to return the bowel to the abdominal cavity at the bedside. Dry coverage with delayed reassessment does not protect the exposed tissue adequately or address the emergency, and packing or treating the exposed bowel with an antiseptic solution is not the recommended emergency management. The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan includes focused assessment, recognition of changes in condition, evaluation of responses to procedures, and prevention of procedure-related complications under Reduction of Risk Potential. Therefore A is the uniquely best answer.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Recognize postoperative abdominal evisceration as a surgical emergency; protect exposed bowel with sterile saline-moistened gauze and obtain urgent surgical evaluation rather than attempting bedside replacement.

semantic_correction.source_locator: NCBI Fascial Dehiscence > Etiology/Evaluation — evisceration is a true surgical emergency and requires emergent surgical evaluation; Treatment/Management — if evisceration occurs, bowel should be wrapped in gauze moistened with saline and the patient prepared for emergent abdominal exploration. NCBI Wound Dehiscence > Issues of Concern — deep fascial dehiscence is a surgical emergency; if evisceration is present, cover the wound with a sterile saline dressing until definitive surgical reduction. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan > Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p. 13 / PDF p. 17 — perform focused assessments; recognize changes in condition and intervene; evaluate responses to procedures/treatments; use precautions to prevent procedure-related complications.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: retired another near-miss-reporting item because that construct was already covered by Q1063. Rebuilt this UID into a distinct postoperative complication requiring immediate tissue protection and surgical escalation.

audit_findings_append.finding: The replacement tests a direct postoperative emergency response. Current NCBI guidance supports saline-moistened coverage and emergent surgical evaluation without bedside replacement of exposed bowel.

scope_exclusions.bedside_reduction: The item explicitly avoids instructing the RN to manually return exposed bowel to the abdominal cavity; definitive reduction is surgical management.
scope_exclusions.positioning: No universal bed position or knee-flexion instruction is asserted because the core tested actions are tissue protection and urgent surgical escalation.
scope_exclusions.antibiotics: No antibiotic regimen is generalized; antimicrobial management depends on the clinical context and surgical evaluation.
scope_exclusions.timing_window: No postoperative-day range is used as a diagnostic requirement; the complication is recognized from the observed wound finding.

near_duplicate_check.note: Targeted GitHub search for 'evisceration saline moist dressing abdominal incision' returned no indexed repository match. No broad bank rescan was performed.

option_audit.A: Correct. It protects exposed bowel with saline-moistened sterile gauze and obtains urgent surgical evaluation, matching current NCBI guidance.
option_audit.B: Plausible impulse to restore anatomy, but exposed bowel should not be manually reduced at the bedside; urgent surgical management is required.
option_audit.C: Plausible wound-support approach for less severe wound problems, but dry coverage and delayed reassessment are inadequate for active evisceration.
option_audit.D: Plausible wound-care response in other contexts, but antiseptic irrigation and packing are not the recommended emergency protection for exposed bowel.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible best answer. The stem explicitly shows bowel through an opened postoperative abdominal wound. A alone combines the source-supported immediate tissue protection with urgent surgical escalation; B attempts bedside reduction and C/D do not provide appropriate emergency management.

cueing_check.note: Exact character counts were calculated from the stored strings. All four options are within seven characters and use parallel wound-management actions.
